module_title: Elastic Load Balancing, Routing and Target Health
review_basis: Individually visually inspected original SAP Module 08 WebP slides 19–21, including all four security panels, four diagnostic steps and five ingress selection criteria.
part_title: Load Balancer Security, Ingress Diagnostics and Design Selection

scenes.title: Secure both the entry point and the target
scenes.visual_overview: The central shield joins four security boundaries: ALB WAF protection, NLB security groups, target reachability and forwarded-header trust.
visual_walkthrough: Upper left: distinguish WAF application request inspection from ALB security-group network access
Upper right: explain why selecting an NLB security group during creation matters
Lower left: allow target application and health-check ports from the load balancer while auditing outbound and stateless NACL return paths
Lower right: examine X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Port without treating user-provided headers as trustworthy identity
scenes.visual_example: An internet ALB fronts private instances. WAF evaluates eligible HTTP traffic, the ALB and targets enforce security groups, and the application trusts forwarded identity hints only through a controlled proxy chain.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Protect both ingress and target boundaries; network reachability and user identity are distinct.
scenes.narration: This diagram makes the case for layered ingress security: the entry point and the target both need protection. Start in the upper-left panel. An Application Load Balancer can integrate with AWS WAF to inspect and filter supported HTTP requests. Its security group instead governs network connectivity, so WAF does not replace those rules. In the upper-right, notice the Network Load Balancer security-group warning. If the NLB is created without a security group, you cannot simply attach one afterward. That decision belongs in initial design and provisioning. Now follow the lower-left panel to the application targets. Where supported, configure target security-group inbound rules to reference the load balancer security group on application and health-check ports. Also examine outbound permissions and the stateless network ACL return path if health checks fail. Finally, the lower-right panel shows forwarded headers such as X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Port. These convey proxy context, not authenticated identity by themselves, and clients may supply misleading values. For example, a public ALB routing to private instances should prevent direct target bypass while separately enforcing application authentication. The decision is to secure each layer rather than assuming one protected listener protects the entire request.

scenes.title: Diagnose ingress with evidence
scenes.visual_overview: Four numbered panels organize an ingress incident investigation around target health, error ownership, metrics and request tracing.
visual_walkthrough: First read target health reason codes, listener and check path, expected response, routes, security groups and NACLs
Separate errors produced by the load balancer from errors produced by a target application
Correlate healthy target counts, request rates, latency, errors and ALB access logs delivered to configured destinations
Trace TLS, listener rule, target registration, application and downstream dependencies; validate one specific fix
scenes.visual_example: A new release returns HTTP 503 to users while a dashboard still shows a provisioned ALB. Inspect healthy-target count and the target-group reason codes before changing listener rules or infrastructure.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A healthy load-balancer resource does not establish that requests succeed; isolate the failing boundary from evidence.
scenes.narration: This slide shows a structured way to troubleshoot an ingress failure without guessing. Begin at step one on the upper-left. Read the target group's health state and reason code, then verify the health-check protocol, port, path and expected response. Confirm security groups, routes and stateless network ACL rules along the probe path. Step two, in the upper-right, asks where the error was produced. A load-balancer-generated error is not the same as an HTTP error returned by a target, and the distinction narrows the investigation. At step three, connect the center monitoring view to CloudWatch metrics: healthy target counts, request volume, response times and error rates. Use ALB access logs where enabled to inspect individual requests and their outcomes; conventional access-log delivery uses S3, with additional supported integrations depending on configuration. Finally, follow step four's request chain through TLS negotiation, listener rule matching, target registration, application logs and dependencies. Consider a deployment that begins returning five-oh-three responses. Before changing every security group, check whether there are any healthy targets and whether the application health path was changed. Fix that specific cause and retest the original client request. The bottom reminder is critical: a green load balancer icon is not proof the user's transaction is working.

scenes.title: Choose ingress for the actual requirement
scenes.visual_overview: Five numbered selection panels contrast HTTP routing, NLB-to-ALB combination, end-to-end TLS, GWLB appliance inspection and cost tradeoffs.
visual_walkthrough: Panel one: ALB consolidates HTTP services with host and path routing
Panel two: NLB-to-ALB combines static zonal entry addresses or PrivateLink with application routing where supported
Panel three: NLB TCP listener passes encrypted traffic when the target needs to terminate the client's TLS session
Panel four: GWLB transparently inserts a compatible appliance fleet using routing and flow consistency
Panel five: compare quotas, scale, data transfer, public IPv4, logging and usage costs before selecting
scenes.visual_example: A private API needs partner access through PrivateLink as well as path-based routing. An NLB with an ALB target may meet both needs; an ordinary multi-service website usually needs only ALB.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Choose the simplest ingress architecture that satisfies protocol, security, availability and operating requirements.
scenes.narration: The final slide turns the previous mechanisms into an architecture decision. First, for several web applications needing host-based or path-based routing behind one entry point, choose an Application Load Balancer. Its HTTP awareness is often the simplest fit. In panel two, the request changes: what if stable zonal IP addresses or PrivateLink must coexist with ALB routing? A supported Network Load Balancer to Application Load Balancer configuration can combine those capabilities, but introduces a second load balancer, additional health checks and cost. Panel three asks who must terminate TLS. If the application target needs to receive and terminate the original encrypted session, a compatible NLB TCP listener can pass through that traffic instead of terminating TLS at the NLB. Panel four is a completely different category. Gateway Load Balancer is for transparent integration with eligible inspection appliance fleets. It depends on explicit forwarding and return routes and consistent flow handling; it is not a replacement for an HTTP ingress controller. Panel five adds practical architecture economics: account for capacity, quotas, transfer, logging, public IPv4 and load balancer charges, using current pricing instead of old assumptions. Suppose a partner needs a private API over PrivateLink but also requires path routing. The NLB-to-ALB composition is plausible. If that requirement disappears, use the simpler ALB-only design. The exam principle is to select the least complex service combination that really meets the requirements.
